claims.text: Increasing oxygen exposure during high-temperature sliding induces a continuous protective oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
The oxygen-induced protective oxide layer promotes dynamic recrystallization at the coating surface.
Dynamic recrystallization produces a refined surface grain structure.
The protective oxide layer and refined grain structure reduce wear relative to low-oxygen exposure.
The protective oxide layer and refined grain structure reduce microscopic deformation relative to low-oxygen exposure.
Air provides the high-oxygen test environment, while argon provides the inert comparison environment.
Thermal activation at high temperature enables oxidation and dynamic recrystallization during sliding.
Frictional heat accelerates oxidation in an oxidizing environment.
The refined surface microstructure limits plastic deformation under sliding contact.
Insufficient oxidation under inert conditions prevents the proposed surface microstructural evolution.
Argon testing will produce higher wear than air testing.
Argon testing will produce more severe microscopic deformation than air testing.
The predictions apply only where oxidation kinetics and dynamic recrystallization are both thermally activated.
The predicted behavior may deviate at lower temperatures or under different mechanical loads.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis frames the intervention as enhanced oxygen relative to low oxygen, but the stated baseline is already air and the experimental comparison uses air as the high-oxygen condition. Thus, relative to the declared baseline, the controlled change is actually oxygen reduction by switching to argon rather than oxygen enhancement.
